Township Spaza Shops

By: Johann Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Spaza shops may hold the key to the xenophobic problem in our townshps

Summary:
Almost all xenophobic outbreaks in South Africa start around foreign owned Spazas. Somehow the foreign nationals can sell their goods for cheaper than anybody else, thus putting local owned shop owners out of business. But how do they do it? Are they simply better businessmen or are they perhaps selling stolen goods?

Further information:
The story falls into two parts: First we investigate claims that Ethiopian and Somali spaza owners in Soweto sell goods from highjackings and warehouse robberies, enabling them to lower their prices to even below production cost. We even speak to a highjacker who works for the Ethiopian mafia, but in the end can't prove it conclusively. Part two takes place in marapong township of lephalale in limpopo, where police acted unlawfully when they closed down all foreign-owned spaza shops. The ethiopians took them to court and wond, but to no avail...

Extra Budget Items:
Trip to Lephalale

Case Study:
Sarah Woldhaane Shop owner

Expert:
Mr. Walter da Costa Displaced and Migrant persons Support Programme

Locations:
Soweto, Gauteng
Lephalale, Limpopo

Press Release:


Township Spaza Shops
As foreign shopkeepers pick up the pieces, questions still linger in the aftermath of the Soweto shop attacks. How do some foreign shop owners manage to sell goods at well below cost price at times? Is there a possible link between corrupt police, truck hijackings and township spaza shops? Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


Short sequence of looting Since 2008 outbursts of Xenophobia had one common denominator. They all started around foreign owned spaza shops, and the fact that they are killing the local owned shops with very low prices and longer opening hours.

But how do they manage to have prices that are sometimes even below production costs?
Visuals of hijackings, warehouses etc Two months ago we exposed a foreign mafia known as The Ethiopians. They are responsible for many truck hijackings, warehouse break-ins and mall robberies. Among the goods they seem to target are regular loads of basic foodstuffs and groceries. Word on the street is that they sell these to some foreign owned spazas at ridiculously low prices, or that they actually own many of these spaza shops and simply stock them in this way..,Although admitting to the losses a number of big companies and their investigators would not talk about this possibility on camera. But we found an insider who works for the syndicate and he adds weight to what would otherwise be only a rumour....
Informant working for the sydicate What they are doing, they are hijacking trucks and stealing groceries for the Ethiopian peoples. They sell it cheaper then. After that they give it to them. Those people from the spaza shop, they sell it cheaper than the South African people.
V/o But while this is quite possibly true for some of the shops, it is obvious that some of the owners work hard at making an honest living.
Mohamed Rshad
Refugee I buy from Makro. I buy from Charoen. I buy from Awash Cash 'n Carry, Jumbo Cash 'n Carry... We've got the card, we can buy from them.
The Chairman of the Somali Business Association believe they they simply outperform the South Africans by working harder and smarter.
Yusuf Mohamed
SA Somali Business Association Many of the Somali businesses are run by entrepreneurs and businessmen who put significant efforts into their businesses. We are talking about people who are open 5am to 11pm 7 days a week just to operate their businesses. Obviously that hard work gives them a competitive edge.
Devi link at Mogadishu I'm in Mogadishu, Mogadishu Johannesburg. This is where many foreign nationals start their new lives in South Africa after fleeing war in their own countries. But in the last week and a half many of them have found themselves in the middle of another war.
Sequence refugee tents in mayfar. Walther giving coment. Other bystanders give comment It is a week since the looting started and a UN contracted agency is busy bringing the chaos under control by regitering all the displaced Somali's who fled here from the townships. Bearing in mind that all of them arrived in South Africa as refugees from near-genocidal conditions in their own countries, this must be like a traumatising flashback for them
Mohamed Rshad
Refugee I come from Ethiopia. My nationality Oromo. Underground, our jail, not even on top. When you're Oromo, you must underground to the jail, or you must get killed.
Walter da Costa goes wherever people are displaced and knows more about what is happening on the ground than most...He believes a lot of the friction around spazas are driven by professional jealousy
Walter da Costa
Displaced and Migrant Persons Support Program They've got very good retail practices because they rotate their stock very fast, being that their stock is very cheap it moves off the shelf very quickly and a first in- first out type of policy on their retail.
Sequence in Soweto In the meantime calm seems to have returned to Soweto. The abandoned shops of the foreigners look as if they've always been this way, and local businessmen are very much aware of the old adage that one man's loss is another man's gain...
Joel Ralgwanasha
Corner Cuisine I feel sorry for them, but it's good for business, you see. I used to order 1 tray of bread. Now I'm ordering about 10 trays, 12 trays now, since they are gone. When they are here I only order 1 tray.
V/o Some of the locals are also outspoken about the Somali's

Local Business owner Did somebody tell the world that if there's a problem wherever you are the only place to come is South Africa?
South African Citizen They are stealing our womans. They are proposing to our womans while our womans come to buy at the spaza shops. That is the cause of some other problem, I think.
Link Devi in Lephalale Turn back the clock to 2012 and lets go to Lephalale in Limpopo. Almost overnight foreign owned spaza shops in the local township of Marapong were shut down.
V/o But this time the perpetrators were not drug crazed youths, but the South African Police Service. Operation Hard Stick struck at businesses without permits across Limpopo.
Walter da Costa
Displaced and Migrant Persons Support Program It was hectic. When they initially came out we were talking about hundreds of shops that were closed down and I think it was almost 2,000 refugees that were affected across Limpopo.
In Lephalale's Marapong township municipal by-laws did not require permits for the township, so no-one had a permit. And still the Police only closed down the foreign owned shops.
Walter da Costa
Displaced and Migrant Persons Support Program The law was applied selectively and they targeted specifically the foreign owned shops.
Walter realised that local businessmen were trying to drive this action to their own advantage.
Walter da Costa
Displaced and Migrant Persons Support Program They've got that power to keep some community members quiet, because they intimidate, they bully. And that is what is happening. They really don't represent the community. The fast majority, we're talking 89 to 89% of the community say yes these people provide us with cheaper goods.
Sarah had her own shop for 5 years in Marapong when the trouble started.
Sarah Woldhaane
Shop owner People liked my shop. Always the customer when they come there they are happy.
The business forum told them to get out, and when they didn't, they broke in and the looting started.
Sarah Woldhaane
Shop owner People they was taking the stock, others with the mealie meal running this side. I don't know what I must do. Just I stop like this, I go to police. Police please help me. I don't have any shop, only this shop. I survive with this shop. Police they tell me no. Us we can't do nothing, just take your things and go.
V/o Sarah and 32 other Ethiopian shop owners decided to take the police to court who ordered them to stop harassing and interfering with their businesses with immediate effect.
Shawn Hamilton
Attorney representing the Ethiopians They then went to the station commander of Lephalale and he then apparently then told them that this court order was a fake and it's kangaroo court. And this matter, he's not going to entertain it. And he'll arrest them if they open up their businesses.
V/o The Police then handed them a very Xenophobic and threatening letter from the Business Forum saying that they must not abuse government resources, that there is no room for illegal immigrants in Marapong, and that the government belongs to South Africans.
Devi Question So, as you stand right now you've got a high court order that doesn't mean anything...
Shawn Hamilton
Attorney representing the Ethiopians I've got 2 high court orders that don't mean anything, because the interim one was then made final.
V/o The police were interdicted and retrained from harassing and interfering with the running of their businesses.
Devi Question What's happening in Lephalale now?
Shawn Hamilton
Attorney representing the Ethiopians None of them have started their businesses because they were told to wait for after the elections when it would be safer, by the station commander, apparently. After the elections they went back to the station commander to ask for assistance to open up the businesses and apparently they've been told it's still too dangerous to open up the businesses and they don't acknowledge those court orders.
Because she lost everything and can't get a job, Sarah now lives with her parents in Vaalwater. She says her three children can't go to school because she hasn't had an income since 2012. Sarah is a South African, and her only sin seems to be that she fell in love and married an Ethiopian.
Sarah Woldhaane
Shop owner This man is my man and I choose him. Out of all people I choose him. Also me I tell myself I was married foreigner. He's my choice.
Sarah's Ethiopian husband is forced to live in Modimolle, where he also has no income. Today, 2 and a half years later, he is once again going to see the police with his court order in his hand. And now they tell him that it is no longer their problem he must now go to the local authority and apply for a business permit on their newly drafted spaza-policy. But it is doubtful if they will be successful, because one of the clauses require that you must own the land on which you run your spaza – so for now there is still no hope for them in sight
Devi Question So, what do you do now?
John Woldhaane For now I don't know because the police don't want to take the court order. Now I don't know now what to do.
Sarah Woldhaane
Shop owner I'm going to survive with what? I was trying to build the house. Now the house has stop. The things I buyed with the credit, they take it back because I don't have money to pay it.
We traced the secretive chairman of the business forum, but he wanted more time to reply. The police simply claimed that they had no knowledge of any such court order and that they deny any wrongdoing. When we sent them a copy of the court order they asked for more time to prepare a new answer. All this explains a disturbing statement that I heard back in Mayfair – that many Somali refugees are now returning to their homeland, chosing to rather face one of the worst wars in recent history than stay in the new land they so proudly say Nelson Mandela promised them.
Yusuf Mohamed
SA Somali Business Association Many have gone back to the war-torn country of Somalia because the condition have become so unbearable. It no longer makes sense safety wise and economic wise to keep on staying in this country.
